description: We are a team of four high schoolers passionate about space exploration, coding, and solving real-world engineering problems.
summary:
RedDot Marswalk is a layered, interactive view of a Marswalk route across Elysium Planitia, answering this challenge's call to fuse decades of robotic Mars data into the best map possible for the first astronauts. Users plan an EVA on a 2D orbital map assembled from real mission data - MRO Context Camera imagery, Viking MDIM 2.1, Mars Express/MGS MOLA blended relief, Odyssey THEMIS thermal infrared, a slope-hazard overlay computed from the 200 m/px blended DEM, and the InSight Marsquake catalog - then switch into a first-person 3D helmet visor built from the same terrain and walk the route manually, on foot or on screen. A safety-first planner engine converts every click into mission numbers: slope-adjusted walking speed benchmarked to the ~1.4 m/s average human pace, an O2 budget with a 40 percent turnaround rule, radiation dose calibrated to MSL RAD measurements, local solar time, and a live GO/NO-GO verdict fed by NOAA space weather. Twelve beaconed science targets, location search with a latitude/longitude fallback, a coordinate grid with true dimensions, live NASA feeds, and a downloadable mission brief complete the tool - free, in any browser, no install required.
Git hub link : https://github.com/terra4nasa/reddot-traverse
details:
What it does and how it works. RedDot Marswalk (ARES-VIS v2.1) is a browser-based Marswalk planner for Elysium Planitia, centred on the InSight landing site 'Homestead Hollow' (about 4.5 degrees N, 135.6 degrees E). In MAP VIEW, the user clicks waypoints on a Leaflet map of real Mars tiles; the app measures haversine distances, samples elevation and slope from a 200 m/px HRSC-MOLA blended DEM, and produces an EVA plan: leg-by-leg timing in local solar time, slope-penalised walking speed, an O2 budget with the 40 percent turnaround rule, cumulative radiation dose, and GO/NO-GO warnings. A coordinate grid with true metre dimensions (about 593 m per 0.01-degree cell at the demo zoom) and a 500 m scale bar keep it readable as an actual map. In VISOR VIEW, a Three.js/WebGL first-person scene renders the same route from the same data: terrain built from the blended DEM, roughly 15,000 instanced rocks, a procedural crater field, a detailed InSight lander model, drifting dust, and sun shadows computed from the true local solar time. A split view shows the 2D map and the visor side by side, and a pulsing beacon marks the astronaut's live position. Twelve beaconed science targets are collected with the E key or the HUD button; dash controls (WASD, SHIFT, drag-to-look, on-screen D-pad) react to the local terrain gradient, benchmarked against the average human walking speed of ~1.4 m/s.

Benefits. It is safety-first by construction: hazards are derived from real elevation data, the O2 budget enforces a turnaround margin before the walk starts, and the GO/NO-GO verdict reflects live space weather, so a route that looks fine on imagery can be correctly rejected. It is honest: every layer shows its mission, instrument, resolution and citation inside the app, and when a live feed is unavailable the panel drops to an explicit STANDBY state instead of pretending. It is free and instant: any judge, teacher or mission enthusiast opens the URL and is walking the route in seconds, with no install and no login. A downloadable mission brief (text plus a GPX track with real elevations) makes plans portable to other tools.

Intended impact. The project demonstrates a repeatable workflow: pick a landing site, fuse optical, topographic, thermal, geophysical, atmospheric and radiation data, then plan a survival-constrained traverse. The layer registry is modular by design - any XYZ/WMTS/GeoJSON endpoint can be added at runtime - so new missions and future datasets plug in without code changes. For classrooms it turns NASA's public archives into a hands-on geography lesson; for planners it sketches how crewed EVAs will consume data from many missions at once.

Tools and technologies. TypeScript; React 19; Next.js 16 (App Router) with serverless API routes; Tailwind CSS 4 with shadcn/Radix UI components; Leaflet and react-leaflet for the map engine; Three.js r187 (WebGL) for the visor; Zustand for state; Vercel for hosting; GitHub Actions for CI. There is no database and no special hardware - any modern desktop or tablet browser works, and touch controls are built in. Live NASA data (Astronomy Picture of the Day, DSCOVR/EPIC full-disc Earth, and the near-Earth-object watch) is fetched through a server-side /api/nasa proxy so the API key never reaches the browser, with in-memory caching to survive many judges viewing at once; space weather comes from NOAA SWPC feeds through a similar proxy, combined with a Keplerian Earth-Mars orbit model that drives the displayed distance and one-way light time.

What makes it creative. The split screen is the signature: the same route exists as an analytical 2D map and as a ground-level 3D visor at the same time, so planners and 'walkers' share one mental model. Six kinds of data are fused into one hyper-local map of a single traverse - optical, topographic, thermal, geophysical, atmospheric and radiation. The visor terrain is not an artist's impression; it is the real DEM, so the hills a user walks in 3D are the hills the planner measured. And the project carries its identity: Singapore's 'Little Red Dot on the Red Planet', mapped at InSight's Homestead Hollow.

Factors considered. Readability and contrast of controls (restyled after early feedback), tablet and touch hardening, speed sensitivity, larger oxygen/suit warning labels, permanent labels that do not require clicks, and a speed hint benchmarked to average human pace. On the data side: cited sources for every layer, approximate epicentres clearly marked as approximate, API keys kept server-side, and graceful degradation to bundled defaults when live feeds fail - because a survival tool that lies is worse than one that admits it is on standby.
